No resource key. No Entra token. No api-version
to track. The app does not even need to know
the model is in Azure, which is what makes a
later move to another provider a config change.

div.div:
• Authenticate the gateway key
• Resolve default-azure
• Check the deployment is on the allowlist
• Check budget and rate limits
• Apply guardrails
• Rewrite the call to the Azure endpoint,
deployment, and API version, then
authenticate with the key or Entra token
• Meter tokens, cost, and latency
• Write the prompt and response log

div.div:
Basic information
Name, Description
Slug default-azure — what the app names in the call
Credential and resource stays here, never handed out
Resource endpoint URL · deployment details · API version, and
either a resource key or an Entra identity with a role on the resource
Model provisioning
The deployments this integration may reach. Everything not on
the list is unreachable through this integration.
Workspace provisioning
Which teams see Azure in their Model Catalog, and each team's
budget and rate limit.
Pricing adjust multiplier
Your enterprise agreement rate, or an internal showback markup.

div.div:
The provider list carries both, and they are not interchangeable.
• Azure OpenAI — your own Azure OpenAI resource, serving the GPT
and embedding deployments you created in your subscription.
• Azure Foundry — Azure's API across a diverse set of foundation
models, including models that are not OpenAI's.
Pick by which resource actually hosts the model the app will call. A team
using both needs two integrations and two slugs, which is also how you
give them two separate budgets.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding-top: 651px; margin-left: 729px;

div.div:
Azure does not serve gpt-4o. It serves a deployment you created and
named, which may be gpt4o-prod, chat-eu, or whatever someone typed
in the portal that afternoon.
That name is what the app puts in the model field, what goes on the
allowlist, and what appears in every log row. Rename it in Azure and
every caller breaks, surfacing as a model-not-found rather than an
auth failure, which sends people looking in the wrong place.
Agree a deployment naming convention before provisioning, for the
same reason you agree the metadata schema before issuing keys.

div.div:
1. Azure bills your subscription for inference. Unchanged by the
gateway. Same resource, same Cost Management line item.
If the resource runs on provisioned throughput rather than
standard pay-as-you-go, that spend is committed capacity and
does not move with token counts at all. The gateway's calculated
cost figures and the Azure invoice will never match, and they are
not supposed to. Use the gateway numbers for allocation between
teams, not for predicting the bill.
2. Palo Alto Networks meters flex credits by token volume.
1 token = 4 characters. Identical pricing for SaaS and Hybrid.

div.div:
The Entra role and endpoint detail come from the repository's key
management guide. The deployment guide explicitly records the Azure
integration form's exact fields as not yet captured, and web research
was blocked in this session. Confirm all of the following:
• Whether the integration form accepts an Entra identity or managed
identity at all, or only a static resource key. This is the difference
between rotating a secret forever and never holding one.
• Whether api-version is a field you set on the integration, or is
pinned by the platform. It changes which request shapes work.
• Whether model provisioning lists deployment names or model names.
• Whether one integration can span several deployments, several
resources, or several regions, or whether each needs its own slug.
• Which Entra role Azure Foundry needs, given that Cognitive Services
OpenAI User is specifically the Azure OpenAI role.
